o.w: Migrating the data into Amazon EFS introduces a different storage service and protocol stack that would require re-architecting the application’s file access, so it does not preserve the same CIFS/NFS protocols the company needs to use in the primary and secondary Regions.

explain: FSx for ONTAP supports NetApp SnapMirror, which is a robust data replication technology. You can use SnapMirror to replicate data from the primary FSx for ONTAP instance in the primary Region to an FSx for ONTAP instance in the secondary Region.

q: A company is creating an application that runs on containers in a VPC. The application stores and accesses data in an Amazon S3 bucket. During the development phase, the application will store and access 1 TB of data in Amazon S3 each day. The company wants to minimize costs and wants to prevent traffic from traversing the internet whenever possible. Which solution will meet these requirements?

o.t: Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration for the S3 bucket
o.w: S3 Transfer Acceleration speeds up uploads over long geographic distances using CloudFront edge locations, but it does not keep traffic off the public internet nor reduce standard data transfer costs for this VPC-based workload.

o.t: Create a gateway VPC endpoint for Amazon S3. Associate this endpoint with all route tables in the VPC
o.w: A gateway VPC endpoint for S3 routes traffic between the VPC and S3 entirely over the AWS private network without traversing the internet, and it has no hourly or per-GB processing charges, making it the most cost-effective choice for this high-volume daily traffic.

o.t: Create an interface endpoint for Amazon S3 in the VPC. Associate this endpoint with all route tables in the VPC
o.w: An interface endpoint for S3 incurs hourly charges and per-GB data processing charges, which is more costly for a high daily volume (1 TB/day) than the free gateway endpoint that already serves S3 traffic within the VPC.

o.t: Enable S3 Intelligent-Tiering for the S3 bucket
o.w: S3 Intelligent-Tiering optimizes storage class costs based on access patterns; it has no effect on network routing or on keeping traffic off the public internet, which is the stated requirement here.

q: A company’s compliance team needs to move its file shares to AWS. The shares run on a Windows Server SMB file share. A self-managed onpremises Active Directory controls access to the files and folders. The company wants to use Amazon FSx for Windows File Server as part of the solution. The company must ensure that the on-premises Active Directory groups restrict access to the FSx for Windows File Server SMB compliance shares, folders, and files after the move to AWS. The company has created an FSx for Windows File Server file system. Which solution will meet these requirements?

o.t: Join the file system to the Active Directory to restrict access.
o.w: Joining the FSx for Windows File Server file system directly to the existing on-premises Active Directory extends the trust relationship to AWS, allowing the existing AD groups to continue controlling access to shares, folders, and files without rebuilding permissions.

o.t: Create an Active Directory Connector to connect to the Active Directory. Map the Active Directory groups to IAM groups to restrict access.
o.w: There is no AWS feature called an "Active Directory Connector" that maps AD groups to IAM groups for FSx access; FSx for Windows File Server access control uses native Windows ACLs tied directly to the joined Active Directory, not IAM groups.

o.t: Create an IAM service-linked role that is linked directly to FSx for Windows File Server to restrict access.
o.w: A service-linked role grants AWS services permission to call other AWS APIs on your behalf; it has no role in controlling SMB-level file and folder access, which is governed by Active Directory, not IAM.

o.t: Assign a tag with a Restrict tag key and a Compliance tag value. Map the Active Directory groups to IAM groups to restrict access.
o.w: Tags are metadata labels used for cost allocation and resource organization; they have no effect on SMB share, folder, or file access control, which depends on Active Directory group permissions.

explain:
Join the File System to Active Directory:

By joining the FSx for Windows File Server file system to the on-premises Active Directory, you extend the trust relationship to AWS.
This ensures that access control is based on the on-premises Active Directory groups, allowing you to continue using the existing groups to restrict access to shares, folders, and files.
After joining the file system to Active Directory, you can manage access controls using the existing Active Directory groups.
Users and groups from the on-premises Active Directory can be granted appropriate permissions on the FSx file system.

q: A company needs to integrate with a third-party data feed. The data feed sends a webhook to notify an external service when new data is ready for consumption. A developer wrote an AWS Lambda function to retrieve data when the company receives a webhook callback. The developer must make the Lambda function available for the third party to call. Which solution will meet these requirements with the MOST operational efficiency?

o.t: Create a function URL for the Lambda function. Provide the Lambda function URL to the third party for the webhook.
o.w: A Lambda function URL exposes the function directly over HTTPS with no additional infrastructure, letting the developer give the third party a simple endpoint to call for the webhook with the least setup and ongoing management.

o.t: Create an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic. Attach the topic to the Lambda function. Provide the public hostname of the SNS topic to the third party for the webhook.
o.w: SNS topics do not expose a public HTTP(S) endpoint that a third party can call directly as a webhook target in the way described; this mischaracterizes how SNS and Lambda integration works for inbound webhook calls.

o.t: Deploy an Application Load Balancer (ALB) in front of the Lambda function. Provide the ALB URL to the third party for the webhook.
o.w: Deploying an ALB in front of a single Lambda function adds an extra piece of infrastructure to provision, configure, and pay for continuously, when a built-in Lambda function URL already provides the needed HTTPS endpoint directly.

o.t: Create an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue. Attach the queue to the Lambda function. Provide the public hostname of the SQS queue to the third party for the webhook.
o.w: SQS queues do not expose a public hostname that an external third party can call as an HTTP webhook; SQS is a pull-based queue, not an inbound HTTP endpoint, so this does not fit the webhook integration pattern described.

explain:
AWS Lambda supports API Gateway integration, which allows you to create an HTTP endpoint (URL) for your Lambda function.
Operational Efficiency:
Directly exposing the Lambda function through a URL eliminates the need for additional services, such as load balancers or message queues, for simple webhook integration.
Simplicity:
This approach is straightforward and easy to implement. It provides a direct URL that the third party can use to invoke the Lambda function when the webhook is triggered.

q: An ecommerce company wants to use machine learning (ML) algorithms to build and train models. The company will use the models to visualize complex scenarios and to detect trends in customer data. The architecture team wants to integrate its ML models with a reporting platform to analyze the augmented data and use the data directly in its business intelligence dashboards. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

o.t: Use Amazon SageMaker to build and train models. Use Amazon QuickSight to visualize the data.
o.w: Amazon SageMaker is a fully managed service for building, training, and deploying ML models, and Amazon QuickSight can connect directly to SageMaker models and visualize their output in BI dashboards, together minimizing operational overhead for this integration.

o.t: Use a pre-built ML Amazon Machine Image (AMI) from the AWS Marketplace to build and train models. Use Amazon OpenSearch Service to visualize the data.
o.w: Pre-built ML AMIs require the company to manage the underlying EC2 infrastructure for model training, and OpenSearch Service is designed for search and log analytics, not for direct business intelligence dashboard integration with ML model output.

o.t: Use AWS Glue to create an ML transform to build and train models. Use Amazon OpenSearch Service to visualize the data.
o.w: AWS Glue ML transforms are limited to specific record-matching/deduplication use cases within ETL jobs, not general-purpose model building and training, and OpenSearch Service is not a natural fit for BI dashboard visualization of ML results.

o.t: Use Amazon QuickSight to build and train models by using calculated fields. Use Amazon QuickSight to visualize the data.
o.w: QuickSight's calculated fields provide basic computed metrics for visualization, not a platform for building and training full machine learning models; this does not meet the requirement to build and train ML models.

explain:
Amazon SageMaker: It is a fully managed service for building, training, and deploying machine learning models. SageMaker simplifies the ML workflow and reduces operational overhead. It provides a fully managed Jupyter Notebook instance for model development and training, and it can seamlessly integrate with other AWS services.
QuickSight can directly connect to Amazon SageMaker models and use the results for visualization without the need for extensive data movement or transformation.

q: A company is implementing a shared storage solution for a media application that is hosted in the AWS Cloud. The company needs the ability to use SMB clients to access data. The solution must be fully managed. Which AWS solution meets these requirements?

o.t: Create an AWS Storage Gateway volume gateway. Create a file share that uses the required client protocol. Connect the application server to the file share.
o.w: AWS Storage Gateway volume gateway presents block storage (iSCSI), not native SMB file shares; it is the file gateway (not volume gateway) configuration that would support SMB, so this option names the wrong Storage Gateway type.

o.t: Create an Amazon FSx for Windows File Server file system. Attach the file system to the origin server. Connect the application server to the file system.
o.w: Amazon FSx for Windows File Server is a fully managed file storage service that natively supports the SMB protocol, giving applications a native Windows file-share experience without having to manage file servers.

o.t: Create an AWS Storage Gateway tape gateway. Configure tapes to use Amazon S3. Connect the application server to the tape gateway.
o.w: AWS Storage Gateway tape gateway is designed for virtual tape backup workflows, not for providing an SMB file share for a media application's live data access needs.

o.t: Create an Amazon EC2 Windows instance. Install and configure a Windows file share role on the instance. Connect the application server to the file share.
o.w: Standing up an EC2 Windows instance with a manually configured file share role requires the company to patch, scale, and manage the server itself, which does not meet the "fully managed" requirement.

explain: Amazon FSx for Windows File Server is a fully managed file storage service that supports the SMB protocol. It provides a native Windows file system experience and is designed to be accessed by SMB clients. This option meets the requirements for a fully managed shared storage solution accessible via SMB.

q: A solutions architect needs to host a high performance computing (HPC) workload in the AWS Cloud. The workload will run on hundreds of Amazon EC2 instances and will require parallel access to a shared file system to enable distributed processing of large datasets. Datasets will be accessed across multiple instances simultaneously. The workload requires access latency within 1 ms. After processing has completed, engineers will need access to the dataset for manual postprocessing. Which solution will meet these requirements?

o.t: Mount an Amazon S3 bucket to serve as the shared file system. Perform postprocessing directly from the S3 bucket.
o.w: Mounting raw S3 as a file system does not provide the POSIX file semantics, parallel access patterns, or sub-millisecond latency needed for tightly coupled HPC workloads; S3 is an object store, not a low-latency parallel file system.

o.t: Configure AWS Resource Access Manager to share an Amazon S3 bucket so that it can be mounted to all instances for processing and postprocessing.
o.w: AWS Resource Access Manager shares AWS resources across accounts; it does not turn an S3 bucket into a low-latency, POSIX-compliant parallel file system suitable for HPC workloads.

o.t: Use Amazon FSx for Lustre as a shared file system. Link the file system to an Amazon S3 bucket for postprocessing.
o.w: FSx for Lustre is purpose-built for HPC, providing sub-millisecond latencies and parallel access across hundreds of instances, and its native S3 integration lets engineers access the same dataset afterward directly through the linked S3 bucket for postprocessing.

o.t: Use Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) as a shared file system. Access the dataset from Amazon EFS.
o.w: Amazon EFS, while a shared POSIX file system, does not provide the sub-millisecond latency and massively parallel throughput characteristics of a purpose-built HPC file system like FSx for Lustre.

explain: FSx for Lustre is designed for high-performance computing workloads that require fast and scalable shared storage. It provides low-latency access to data and is well-suited for parallel processing across multiple instances.

q: A company manages its own Amazon EC2 instances that run MySQL databases. The company is manually managing replication and scaling as demand increases or decreases. The company needs a new solution that simplifies the process of adding or removing compute capacity to or from its database tier as needed. The solution also must offer improved performance, scaling, and durability with minimal effort from operations. Which solution meets these requirements?

o.t: Migrate the databases to Amazon Aurora Serverless for Aurora PostgreSQL.
o.w: Aurora Serverless for Aurora PostgreSQL would require migrating from a MySQL engine to a different database engine (PostgreSQL), which is a far bigger and riskier change than simply moving to the matching MySQL-compatible Aurora engine.

o.t: Combine the databases into one larger MySQL database. Run the larger database on larger EC2 instances.
o.w: Combining databases into one larger self-managed MySQL database on bigger EC2 instances still requires the company to manually manage replication, scaling, and durability, directly failing to reduce the described operational burden.

o.t: Migrate the databases to Amazon Aurora Serverless for Aurora MySQL.
o.w: Aurora Serverless for Aurora MySQL automatically scales compute capacity up and down based on demand while remaining compatible with the existing MySQL databases, eliminating manual replication and scaling management with minimal operational effort.

o.t: Create an EC2 Auto Scaling group for the database tier. Migrate the existing databases to the new environment.
o.w: An EC2 Auto Scaling group can scale compute instances but does not provide the built-in database replication, durability, and storage scaling that Aurora provides natively; the company would still be managing MySQL on EC2 manually.

explain: Amazon Aurora Serverless: Aurora Serverless is an on-demand, auto-scaling configuration for Amazon Aurora. It automatically adjusts the database capacity based on actual consumption, enabling seamless scaling without manual intervention. It is a fully managed service, reducing operational overhead.

q: A company recently deployed a new auditing system to centralize information about operating system versions, patching, and installed software for Amazon EC2 instances. A solutions architect must ensure all instances provisioned through EC2 Auto Scaling groups successfully send reports to the auditing system as soon as they are launched and terminated. Which solution achieves these goals MOST efficiently?

o.t: Use an EC2 Auto Scaling launch configuration to run a custom script through user data to send data to the audit system when instances are launched and terminated.
o.w: Launch configurations' user data scripts run once at EC2 boot but have no equivalent built-in hook for instance termination, so this does not reliably capture termination events needed by the audit system.

o.t: Use a scheduled AWS Lambda function and run a script remotely on all EC2 instances to send data to the audit system.
o.w: Using a Lambda function to poll or run scripts remotely on all instances on a schedule is inefficient and does not tie directly to the precise moments instances launch or terminate, risking missed or delayed audit reports.

o.t: Use EC2 Auto Scaling lifecycle hooks to run a custom script to send data to the audit system when instances are launched and terminated.
o.w: EC2 Auto Scaling lifecycle hooks pause instances in a Pending or Terminating state and let you run a custom action, such as sending data to the audit system, exactly at launch and termination, which is the native, efficient mechanism for this exact use case.

o.t: Run a custom script on the instance operating system to send data to the audit system. Configure the script to be invoked by the EC2 Auto Scaling group when the instance starts and is terminated.
o.w: Relying on the instance's own OS-level script tied to Auto Scaling's termination notice is less reliable than a proper lifecycle hook, since the instance may already be shutting down and cannot guarantee the script completes and reports before termination finishes.

q: A company provides a Voice over Internet Protocol (VoIP) service that uses UDP connections. The service consists of Amazon EC2 instances that run in an Auto Scaling group. The company has deployments across multiple AWS Regions. The company needs to route users to the Region with the lowest latency. The company also needs automated failover between Regions. Which solution will meet these requirements?

o.t: Deploy an Application Load Balancer (ALB) and an associated target group. Associate the target group with the Auto Scaling group. Create an Amazon Route 53 weighted record that points to aliases for each ALB. Deploy an Amazon CloudFront distribution that uses the weighted record as an origin.
o.w: ALBs and CloudFront operate at Layer 7 and do not support UDP, which this VoIP service requires; this architecture is fundamentally incompatible with the UDP-based workload.

o.t: Deploy a Network Load Balancer (NLB) and an associated target group. Associate the target group with the Auto Scaling group. Create an Amazon Route 53 latency record that points to aliases for each NLB. Create an Amazon CloudFront distribution that uses the latency record as an origin.
o.w: Route 53 latency-based routing combined with CloudFront is unnecessary and incompatible, since CloudFront does not support UDP traffic, and Global Accelerator (not a Route 53 latency record plus CloudFront) is the AWS service designed for automated low-latency Regional failover of UDP workloads.

o.t: Deploy an Application Load Balancer (ALB) and an associated target group. Associate the target group with the Auto Scaling group. Use the ALB as an AWS Global Accelerator endpoint in each Region.
o.w: An ALB does not support UDP traffic, which this VoIP application requires, so fronting the Auto Scaling group with an ALB is incompatible with the workload's protocol.

o.t: Deploy a Network Load Balancer (NLB) and an associated target group. Associate the target group with the Auto Scaling group. Use the NLB as an AWS Global Accelerator endpoint in each Region.
o.w: A Network Load Balancer supports UDP traffic required by the VoIP service, and AWS Global Accelerator automatically routes users to the Region with the lowest latency using Anycast IPs while providing automated health-check-based failover between Regions, directly meeting both requirements.

explain:
Answer A does not mention service Global Accelerator, it mentions the NLB would act like one. Not sure if the wording is wrong or not.
' Deploy a Network Load Balancer (NLB) and an associated target group. Associate the target group with the Auto Scaling group. Use the NLB as an AWS Global Accelerator endpoint in each Region.

q: A company created a new organization in AWS Organizations. The organization has multiple accounts for the company's development teams. The development team members use AWS IAM Identity Center (AWS Single Sign-On) to access the accounts. For each of the company's applications, the development teams must use a predefined application name to tag resources that are created. A solutions architect needs to design a solution that gives the development team the ability to create resources only if the application name tag has an approved value. Which solution will meet these requirements?

o.t: Create an IAM group that has a conditional Allow policy that requires the application name tag to be specified for resources to be created.
o.w: An IAM policy with a conditional Allow based on a tag value must be written, tested, and maintained per group/policy, and does not centrally enforce an approved list of tag values across the whole organization the way a native Organizations feature can.

o.t: Create a tag policy in Organizations that has a list of allowed application names.
o.w: AWS Organizations tag policies let you define an explicit list of allowed values for a given tag key (such as application name) and enforce compliance across accounts, directly meeting the requirement to allow resource creation only with an approved tag value.

o.t: Create a resource group in AWS Resource Groups to validate that the tags are applied to all resources in all accounts.
o.w: AWS Resource Groups with tag validation can report on which resources are tagged correctly, but it is a reporting/auditing tool, not a preventive control that blocks resource creation with a disallowed tag value.

o.t: Create a cross-account role that has a Deny policy for any resource that has the application name tag.
o.w: A cross-account Deny policy targeting any resource with the application name tag would block all tagged resources, including ones with approved tag values, rather than selectively allowing only approved values.

q: A global video streaming company uses Amazon CloudFront as a content distribution network (CDN). The company wants to roll out content in a phased manner across multiple countries. The company needs to ensure that viewers who are outside the countries to which the company rolls out content are not able to view the content. Which solution will meet these requirements?

o.t: Create a new URL for restricted content. Set up a time-restricted access policy for signed URLs.
o.w: Signed URLs with time-based restrictions control when content can be accessed, not where viewers are located, so they do not meet the geographic restriction requirement.

o.t: Set up a new URL tor restricted content. Authorize access by using a signed URL and cookies. Set up a custom error message.
o.w: Signed URLs and cookies control authorization based on user credentials and expiry, not the geographic location of the viewer, so this does not prevent access from unauthorized countries.

o.t: Add geographic restrictions to the content in CloudFront by using an allow list. Set up a custom error message.
o.w: CloudFront's geographic restriction feature lets you specify an allow list of countries permitted to view content, and a custom error message can be shown to blocked viewers, directly meeting the phased rollout and geo-blocking requirements.

o.t: Encrypt the data for the content that the company distributes. Set up a custom error message.
o.w: Encrypting the content controls confidentiality of the data itself but does not control or restrict which geographic locations are permitted to retrieve and view that content.

explain: CloudFront allows you to set up geographic restrictions by creating an allow list. This allows you to specify the countries from which viewers are allowed to access your content. Viewers from countries not in the allow list will be restricted from accessing the content.

q: A rapidly growing ecommerce company is running its workloads in a single AWS Region. A solutions architect must create a disaster recovery (DR) strategy that includes a different AWS Region. The company wants its database to be up to date in the DR Region with the least possible latency. The remaining infrastructure in the DR Region needs to run at reduced capacity and must be able to scale up if necessary. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LOWEST recovery time objective (RTO)?

o.t: Use an Amazon Aurora global database with a warm standby deployment.
o.w: An Aurora global database replicates data to the secondary Region with typical latency under a second, and a warm standby deployment keeps resources running at reduced capacity in the DR Region so they can scale up quickly, achieving the lowest RTO among the options.

o.t: Use an Amazon Aurora global database with a pilot light deployment.
o.w: A pilot light deployment keeps only minimal/core resources running (such as just the database) in the DR Region, requiring the remaining infrastructure to be provisioned from scratch during failover, which results in a higher RTO than a warm standby that already has infrastructure running.

o.t: Use an Amazon RDS Multi-AZ DB instance with a warm standby deployment.
o.w: RDS Multi-AZ instances provide high availability within a Region via a standby in another AZ, not cross-Region replication; this does not meet the requirement for an up-to-date database in a separate DR Region.

o.t: Use an Amazon RDS Multi-AZ DB instance with a pilot light deployment.
o.w: RDS Multi-AZ instances replicate only within a Region, not to a separate DR Region, and a pilot light approach additionally requires building up infrastructure during failover, resulting in a much higher RTO than required.

explain:
Amazon Aurora supports a global database feature that allows you to create read replicas in multiple AWS Regions.
In a warm standby deployment, you can have a read replica in the DR Region that stays warm, meaning it is ready to take over in case of a failover.

q: A company hosts a three-tier web application in the AWS Cloud. A Multi-AZAmazon RDS for MySQL server forms the database layer Amazon ElastiCache forms the cache layer. The company wants a caching strategy that adds or updates data in the cache when a customer adds an item to the database. The data in the cache must always match the data in the database. Which solution will meet these requirements?

o.t: Implement the write-through caching strategy
o.w: In the write-through strategy, the cache is updated at the same time as the database write, so the data in the cache always matches the data in the database immediately after each write, exactly meeting the stated consistency requirement.

o.t: Implement the adding TTL caching strategy
o.w: TTL-based expiration only removes stale data after a fixed time passes; it does not update the cache the moment the database is written to, so the cache can be out of sync with the database until the TTL expires.

o.t: Implement the AWS AppConfig caching strategy
o.w: AWS AppConfig is a feature flag and configuration management service; it is not a caching strategy for keeping an ElastiCache layer synchronized with RDS data changes.

o.t: Implement the lazy loading caching strategy
o.w: In lazy loading, the cache is only updated when an application requests data and finds a cache miss, meaning the cache can remain outdated until the next read, so it does not guarantee the cache always matches the database immediately after a write.

explain:
In a write-through caching strategy, data is always written or updated in the cache when it is modified in the database. This ensures that the cache is consistently updated with the latest data from the database.
When a customer adds an item to the database, the write-through caching strategy ensures that the item is also added or updated in the cache.

q: A development team is creating an event-based application that uses AWS Lambda functions. Events will be generated when files are added to an Amazon S3 bucket. The development team currently has Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) configured as the event target from Amazon S3. What should a solutions architect do to process the events from Amazon S3 in a scalable way?

o.t: Create an SNS subscription that processes the event in Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) before the event runs in Lambda.
o.w: Processing the event in ECS before it reaches Lambda adds an extra compute layer to manage and scale, which is unnecessary complexity for an event-driven workflow that should remain fully serverless and simple.

o.t: Create an SNS subscription that processes the event in Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) before the event runs in Lambda
o.w: Processing the event in EKS before Lambda introduces a Kubernetes cluster to provision and manage, which is a far heavier operational footprint than simply decoupling S3/SNS events from Lambda with a managed queue.

o.t: Create an SNS subscription that sends the event to Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS). Configure the SOS queue to trigger a Lambda function.
o.w: Routing the SNS notification into an SQS queue and configuring that queue to trigger Lambda decouples event delivery from processing, letting SQS buffer bursts of S3 events so the function scales and processes messages reliably, which is the standard scalable SNS fan-out-to-Lambda pattern.

o.t: Create an SNS subscription that sends the event to AWS Server Migration Service (AWS SMS). Configure the Lambda function to poll from the SMS event.
o.w: AWS Server Migration Service is used to migrate on-premises VMs to AWS; it has no role in routing S3-triggered application events to a Lambda function and does not even support a Lambda polling pattern.

q: A company has an application that provides marketing services to stores. The services are based on previous purchases by store customers. The stores upload transaction data to the company through SFTP, and the data is processed and analyzed to generate new marketing offers. Some of the files can exceed 200 GB in size. Recently, the company discovered that some of the stores have uploaded files that contain personally identifiable information (PII) that should not have been included. The company wants administrators to be alerted if PII is shared again. The company also wants to automate remediation. What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements with the LEAST development effort?

o.t: Implement custom scanning algorithms in an AWS Lambda function. Trigger the function when objects are loaded into the bucket. If objects contain PII, use Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) to trigger a notification to the administrators to remove the objects that contain PII.
o.w: Writing custom PII-scanning algorithms in Lambda requires significant development effort to build, test, and maintain pattern-matching logic that a managed service already provides, failing the "least development effort" requirement.

o.t: Use an Amazon S3 bucket as a secure transfer point. Use Amazon Macie to scan the objects in the bucket. If objects contain PII, use Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) to trigger a notification to the administrators to remove the objects that contain PII.
o.w: Amazon Macie is a managed service purpose-built to automatically discover and alert on sensitive data such as PII in S3 buckets, and pairing it with SNS to notify administrators meets the requirement with minimal custom development.

o.t: Use an Amazon S3 bucket as a secure transfer point. Use Amazon Inspector to scan the objects in the bucket. If objects contain PII, trigger an S3 Lifecycle policy to remove the objects that contain PII.
o.w: Amazon Inspector is designed to assess EC2 instances and container images for software vulnerabilities, not to scan S3 object content for PII, so it does not fit this use case, and automatically deleting flagged objects via a lifecycle policy removes evidence before investigation/remediation can occur.

o.t: Implement custom scanning algorithms in an AWS Lambda function. Trigger the function when objects are loaded into the bucket. If objects contain PII, use Amazon Simple Email Service (Amazon SES) to trigger a notification to the administrators and trigger an S3 Lifecycle policy to remove the meats that contain PII.
o.w: Building custom PII-scanning Lambda code requires substantial development effort that a managed service like Macie avoids, and automatically deleting flagged files via a lifecycle policy removes the objects before administrators can review and properly remediate them.

explain: Some quotas can be increased, while others cannot. To request an increase to a quota, use the Service Quotas console. To learn how to request an increase, see Requesting a quota increase in the Service Quotas User Guide. If a quota isn't available on the Service Quotas console, use the service limit increase form on the AWS Support Center Console to request an increase to the quota.

q: A gaming company uses Amazon DynamoDB to store user information such as geographic location, player data, and leaderboards. The company needs to configure continuous backups to an Amazon S3 bucket with a minimal amount of coding. The backups must not affect availability of the application and must not affect the read capacity units (RCUs) that are defined for the table. Which solution meets these requirements?

o.t: Create an AWS Lambda function to export the data from the database tables to Amazon S3 on a regular basis. Turn on point-in-time recovery for the table.
o.w: A custom Lambda export script requires the company to write and maintain scheduling and export code, which is more development effort than the minimal-coding requirement calls for, even though point-in-time recovery itself is appropriately enabled here.

o.t: Use an Amazon EMR cluster. Create an Apache Hive job to back up the data to Amazon S3.
o.w: Standing up an EMR cluster with a custom Hive job to export DynamoDB data requires significant infrastructure management and custom coding, which conflicts with the goal of minimal coding effort.

o.t: Configure Amazon DynamoDB Streams. Create an AWS Lambda function to consume the stream and export the data to an Amazon S3 bucket.
o.w: Using DynamoDB Streams with a custom Lambda consumer to export data to S3 requires writing and maintaining stream-processing code, which is more development effort than using DynamoDB's built-in continuous S3 export feature.

o.t: Export the data directly from DynamoDB to Amazon S3 with continuous backups. Turn on point-in-time recovery for the table.
o.w: DynamoDB's native continuous export to S3 feature streams table data to S3 without consuming any provisioned RCUs or affecting table availability, and enabling point-in-time recovery alongside it meets the backup requirement with minimal coding.

q: A company hosts a frontend application that uses an Amazon API Gateway API backend that is integrated with AWS Lambda. When the API receives requests, the Lambda function loads many libraries. Then the Lambda function connects to an Amazon RDS database, processes the data, and returns the data to the frontend application. The company wants to ensure that response latency is as low as possible for all its users with the fewest number of changes to the company's operations. Which solution will meet these requirements?

o.t: Cache the results of the queries in Amazon S3 for faster retrieval of similar datasets.
o.w: Caching query results in S3 would require custom application logic to check and update the cache and does not address the root cause of latency, which is Lambda's cold-start initialization time from loading many libraries.

o.t: Establish a connection between the frontend application and the database to make queries faster by bypassing the API.
o.w: Bypassing the API and connecting the frontend directly to the database removes the processing logic the Lambda function performs and introduces security and architecture risks; it does not address the stated cold-start latency issue and requires significant changes to company operations.

o.t: Increase the size of the database to increase the number of connections Lambda can establish at one time.
o.w: Increasing database size affects how many connections the database can handle, not how quickly the Lambda function initializes and loads its libraries, so it does not address the described latency cause.

o.t: Configure provisioned concurrency for the Lambda function that handles the requests.
o.w: Provisioned concurrency keeps a set number of Lambda execution environments pre-initialized with the function's libraries already loaded, eliminating the cold-start delay with a single configuration change and no changes to application code or operations.

explain: Provisioned Concurrency: Provisioned concurrency allows you to pre-warm a specific number of instances of your Lambda function. This ensures that there are already instances available to handle incoming requests, reducing the cold start latency. Since the Lambda function loads many libraries, reducing cold start latency is crucial for optimizing response time.

q: A company provides an online service for posting video content and transcoding it for use by any mobile platform. The application architecture uses Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) Standard to collect and store the videos so that multiple Amazon EC2 Linux instances can access the video content for processing. As the popularity of the service has grown over time, the storage costs have become too expensive. Which storage solution is MOST cost-effective?

o.t: Use AWS Storage Gateway for volumes to store and process the video content.
o.w: AWS Storage Gateway volume gateway is meant for presenting block storage to on-premises or EC2 environments; it does not reduce the cost of storing large volumes of video content the way object storage does, and processing directly on gateway volumes is not its intended use.

o.t: Use Amazon S3 for storing the video content. Move the files temporarily over to an Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volume attached to the server for processing.
o.w: Storing the master video content in low-cost Amazon S3 and only temporarily copying files to EBS for active processing significantly reduces storage costs compared to keeping everything in EFS Standard, while still letting EC2 instances process the files efficiently.

o.t: Use Amazon EFS for storing the video content. Once processing is complete, transfer the files to Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS).
o.w: Simply moving storage to EFS does not reduce costs, since EFS Standard is what the company is already using and finding too expensive; transferring processed files to EBS afterward does not solve the underlying storage cost problem.

o.t: Use AWS Storage Gateway for files to store and process the video content.
o.w: AWS Storage Gateway file gateway, like the volume gateway option, is intended for presenting files from S3 to on-premises or hybrid environments rather than being the most cost-effective solution for storing and directly processing large video files from EC2 at this scale.

explain:
Amazon S3 is a highly durable, scalable, and cost-effective object storage service.
It is well-suited for storing large amounts of video content at a lower cost compared to Amazon EFS.

q: A company wants to use an Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL DB cluster to simplify time-consuming database administrative tasks for production database workloads. The company wants to ensure that its database is highly available and will provide automatic failover support in most scenarios in less than 40 seconds. The company wants to offload reads off of the primary instance and keep costs as low as possible. Which solution will meet these requirements?

o.t: Use an Amazon RDS Multi-AZ DB instance deployment. Create one read replica and point the read workload to the read replica.
o.w: A Multi-AZ DB instance with a separate read replica adds replica lag and extra replica infrastructure cost, and typical Multi-AZ instance failover times, while fast, are generally not as tightly bounded as the DB cluster deployment's sub-40-second failover with an integrated reader endpoint.

o.t: Use an Amazon RDS Multi-AZ DB instance deployment. Point the read workload to the secondary instances in the Multi-AZ pair.
o.w: Pointing reads directly at the secondary (standby) instance of a Multi-AZ DB instance deployment is not supported for RDS Multi-AZ instance deployments; the standby is not readable, so this architecture does not actually offload reads as intended.

o.t: Use an Amazon RDS Multi-AZ DB cluster deployment Point the read workload to the reader endpoint.
o.w: An RDS Multi-AZ DB cluster deployment provides automatic failover typically in under 35 seconds and includes built-in readable standby instances accessible through a reader endpoint, letting reads be offloaded from the primary without the extra cost of separate read replicas.

o.t: Use an Amazon RDS Multi-AZ DB duster deployment Create two read replicas and point the read workload to the read replicas.
o.w: Creating two additional read replicas on top of a Multi-AZ DB cluster deployment adds unnecessary extra cost, since the Multi-AZ DB cluster's built-in reader endpoint already provides read scaling without additional replica instances.

explain: Amazon RDS Multi-AZ DB Cluster Deployment: This provides high availability by automatically replicating data to a standby instance in a different Availability Zone. In case of a failure, Amazon RDS automatically fails over to the standby instance.

q: A company is hosting a web application on AWS using a single Amazon EC2 instance that stores user-uploaded documents in an Amazon EBS volume. For better scalability and availability, the company duplicated the architecture and created a second EC2 instance and EBS volume in another Availability Zone, placing both behind an Application Load Balancer. After completing this change, users reported that, each time they refreshed the website, they could see one subset of their documents or the other, but never all of the documents at the same time. What should a solutions architect propose to ensure users see all of their documents at once?

o.t: Configure the Application Load Balancer to direct a user to the server with the documents
o.w: An ALB uses routing algorithms to distribute requests across targets and has no awareness of which specific files reside on which backend instance's local EBS volume, so it cannot ensure a user sees all their documents at once.

o.t: Copy the data from both EBS volumes to Amazon EFS. Modify the application to save new documents to Amazon EFS
o.w: Migrating the documents to Amazon EFS gives both EC2 instances concurrent shared access to the same file store, ensuring every request sees the complete, consistent set of documents regardless of which instance handles it.

o.t: Copy the data so both EBS volumes contain all the documents
o.w: Manually copying data between the two EBS volumes only synchronizes the data at that moment; the volumes are not shared in real time, so new uploads to one instance would not immediately appear in the other, and the underlying problem of split-brain storage persists.

o.t: Configure the Application Load Balancer to send the request to both servers. Return each document from the correct server
o.w: An ALB cannot aggregate or merge documents from multiple backend servers into a single response for the end user; this is not how its request routing or response handling works.

explain: Option C, which involves copying the data to Amazon EFS and modifying the application to use Amazon EFS for document storage, is the most appropriate solution to ensure users can see all their documents at once in the duplicated architecture. Amazon EFS provides scalability, availability, and shared access, allowing both EC2 instances to access and synchronize the documents seamlessly. Unlike EBS volumes or snapshots, which cannot be shared in real time across multiple instances and Availability Zones, Amazon EFS allows both EC2 instances to access the same file system simultaneously, ensuring all users see the same set of documents regardless of which instance serves their request.

q: A company operates a two-tier application for image processing. The application uses two Availability Zones, each with one public subnet and one private subnet. An Application Load Balancer (ALB) for the web tier uses the public subnets. Amazon EC2 instances for the application tier use the private subnets. Users report that the application is running more slowly than expected. A security audit of the web server log files shows that the application is receiving millions of illegitimate requests from a small number of IP addresses. A solutions architect needs to resolve the immediate performance problem while the company investigates a more permanent solution. What should the solutions architect recommend to meet this requirement?

o.t: Modify the inbound security group for the application tier. Add a deny rule for the IP addresses that are consuming resources.
o.w: Modifying the application-tier security group does not block the illegitimate traffic, since the attack traffic is hitting the web tier's ALB in the public subnets, not the private application tier directly.

o.t: Modify the inbound security group for the web tier. Add a deny rule for the IP addresses that are consuming resources.
o.w: Security groups are stateful and attached per-instance/resource, and modifying the web tier's security group would need to be done per target; a network ACL at the subnet level more efficiently blocks traffic from specific IP addresses before it reaches any resource in the subnet, making it a more direct quick fix at the network layer for this scenario.

o.t: Modify the network ACL for the web tier subnets. Add an inbound deny rule for the IP addresses that are consuming resources.
o.w: Adding an inbound deny rule in the network ACL for the web tier's public subnets blocks the illegitimate traffic from the specific IP addresses at the subnet boundary before it consumes application resources, providing an immediate mitigation while a permanent solution is investigated.

o.t: Modify the network ACL for the application tier subnets. Add an inbound deny rule for the IP addresses that are consuming resources.
o.w: The illegitimate traffic is hitting the web tier (through the ALB in the public subnets), not the application tier directly, so blocking IPs at the application tier's subnet level would not stop the traffic from reaching and overwhelming the web tier.

q: What should a solutions architect do to ensure that all objects uploaded to an Amazon S3 bucket are encrypted?

o.t: Update the bucket policy to deny if the PutObject does not have an x-amz-server-side-encryption header set.
o.w: Denying any PutObject request that lacks the x-amz-server-side-encryption header forces every uploaded object to specify server-side encryption, ensuring all objects in the bucket are encrypted.

o.t: Update the bucket policy to deny if the PutObject does not have an s3:x-amz-acl header set to private.
o.w: The s3:x-amz-acl header controls object access control list permissions (such as private vs. public-read), not whether the object is encrypted, so this condition does not enforce encryption.

o.t: Update the bucket policy to deny if the PutObject does not have an s3:x-amz-acl header set.
o.w: Requiring the s3:x-amz-acl header to simply be present only ensures an ACL setting was specified; it says nothing about encryption, so uploaded objects could still be stored unencrypted.

o.t: Update the bucket policy to deny if the PutObject does not have an aws:SecureTransport header set to true.
o.w: The aws:SecureTransport condition enforces that requests use HTTPS (encryption in transit), not that the stored object itself is encrypted at rest, so it does not ensure object encryption as required.

explain: x-amz-server-side-encryption header: This header specifies the server-side encryption algorithm to be used for the object. If an object is uploaded without the x-amz-server-side-encryption header or with an incorrect value, it can be denied.

q: A company observes an increase in Amazon EC2 costs in its most recent bill. The billing team notices unwanted vertical scaling of instance types for a couple of EC2 instances. A solutions architect needs to create a graph comparing the last 2 months of EC2 costs and perform an in-depth analysis to identify the root cause of the vertical scaling. How should the solutions architect generate the information with the LEAST operational overhead?

o.t: Use AWS Budgets to create a budget report and compare EC2 costs based on instance types.
o.w: AWS Budgets is designed to track spending against a budget threshold and send alerts; it does not provide the granular historical comparison and root-cause drill-down into which instance types changed that this investigation requires.

o.t: Use AWS Cost and Usage Reports to create a report and send it to an Amazon S3 bucket. Use Amazon QuickSight with Amazon S3 as a source to generate an interactive graph based on instance types.
o.w: Setting up Cost and Usage Reports with S3 and QuickSight for an interactive graph requires building and maintaining a reporting pipeline, which is considerably more operational effort than using a built-in analysis tool that already exists.

o.t: Use graphs from the AWS Billing and Cost Management dashboard to compare EC2 costs based on instance types for the last 2 months.
o.w: The Billing and Cost Management dashboard graphs provide only high-level cost visualizations and lack the granular, interactive filtering needed to drill into specific instance type changes behind the vertical scaling.

o.t: Use Cost Explorer's granular filtering feature to perform an in-depth analysis of EC2 costs based on instance types.
o.w: Cost Explorer provides built-in, granular filtering by service, instance type, and time period directly in the console, letting the solutions architect compare the last 2 months and drill into the root cause of the vertical scaling without building any new reporting infrastructure.

q: A company wants to migrate its web applications from on premises to AWS. The company is located close to the eu-central-1 Region. Because of regulations, the company cannot launch some of its applications in eu-central-1. The company wants to achieve single-digit millisecond latency. Which solution will meet these requirements?

o.t: Deploy the applications in AWS Wavelength Zones by extending the company’s VPC from eu-central-1 to the chosen Wavelength Zone.
o.w: AWS Wavelength Zones are designed to embed compute at telecom providers' 5G network edge for ultra-low-latency mobile applications; they are not the general-purpose mechanism for serving regulated workloads that must stay physically close to a specific metro area outside the parent Region's data center.

o.t: Deploy the applications in AWS Local Zones by extending the company's VPC from eu-central-1 to the chosen Local Zone.
o.w: AWS Local Zones let the company extend its VPC from eu-central-1 to an infrastructure deployment physically closer to end users, achieving single-digit millisecond latency while keeping the workload outside the restricted eu-central-1 Region to satisfy the regulatory constraint.

o.t: Deploy the applications in eu-central-1. Extend the company’s VPC from eu-central-1 to an edge location in Amazon CloudFront.
o.w: CloudFront edge locations cache and accelerate static/dynamic content delivery; they do not let you run full application workloads outside the Region to satisfy a regulatory placement constraint, and the applications still would effectively run in eu-central-1.

o.t: Deploy the applications in eu-central-1. Extend the company’s VPC from eu-central-1 to the regional edge caches in Amazon CloudFront.
o.w: Regional edge caches are an additional CloudFront caching tier for content delivery, not a compute location where applications can be deployed outside the eu-central-1 Region to satisfy the stated regulatory restriction.

q: A company collects data from a large number of participants who use wearable devices. The company stores the data in an Amazon DynamoDB table and uses applications to analyze the data. The data workload is constant and predictable. The company wants to stay at or below its forecasted budget for DynamoDB. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?

o.t: Use provisioned mode and DynamoDB Standard-Infrequent Access (DynamoDB Standard-IA). Reserve capacity for the forecasted workload.
o.w: DynamoDB Standard-IA is intended for infrequently accessed tables to save on storage costs, not for optimizing throughput costs for a constant, predictable workload, and mixing it with reserved capacity does not align with how DynamoDB capacity modes work.

o.t: Use on-demand mode. Specify the read capacity units (RCUs) and write capacity units (WCUs) with reserved capacity.
o.w: On-demand mode does not support "reserving" RCUs/WCUs in the way described; on-demand mode charges per request and has no provisioned reservation mechanism, making this combination inconsistent with how DynamoDB capacity modes actually work.

o.t: Use on-demand mode. Set the read capacity units (RCUs) and write capacity units (WCUs) high enough to accommodate changes in the workload.
o.w: Setting on-demand RCUs/WCUs artificially high does not actually control cost, since on-demand mode bills per request regardless of any capacity setting; this approach does not achieve predictable, budget-aligned costs for a steady workload.

o.t: Use provisioned mode. Specify the read capacity units (RCUs) and write capacity units (WCUs).
o.w: For a constant and predictable workload, provisioned capacity mode lets the company specify exactly the RCUs and WCUs needed, which is more cost-effective than on-demand mode's per-request pricing and keeps spending aligned with the forecasted budget.

explain: In provisioned mode, you provision a specific amount of read and write capacity, which allows you to manage costs more effectively based on your expected workload. This approach is suitable when your workload is predictable, as you can provision the capacity to meet your known requirements. DynamoDB Standard-Infrequent Access (Option A) is designed for cost savings on long-term storage and retrieval of infrequently accessed data, and it might not be the best fit for a constant and predictable workload.

q: A company has two VPCs named Management and Production. The Management VPC uses VPNs through a customer gateway to connect to a single device in the data center. The Production VPC uses a virtual private gateway with two attached AWS Direct Connect connections. The Management and Production VPCs both use a single VPC peering connection to allow communication between the applications. What should a solutions architect do to mitigate any single point of failure in this architecture?

o.t: Add a second virtual private gateway and attach it to the Management VPC.
o.w: Adding a second virtual private gateway to the Management VPC does not address its actual single point of failure, which is the single customer gateway device on the data-center side of its VPN connection, not the AWS-side gateway.

o.t: Add a second VPC peering connection between the Management VPC and the Production VPC.
o.w: A second VPC peering connection would only add redundancy for the peering link between the two VPCs; it does not address the single point of failure in the Management VPC's data-center-side VPN connectivity, which relies on just one customer gateway device.

o.t: Add a set of VPNs between the Management and Production VPCs.
o.w: Routing VPN connections directly between the Management and Production VPCs changes the network design significantly and does not address the real single point of failure, which is the single on-premises customer gateway device used by the Management VPC's existing VPN.

o.t: Add a second set of VPNs to the Management VPC from a second customer gateway device.
o.w: The Management VPC's connectivity relies on a single customer gateway device in the data center; adding a second set of VPNs terminating on a second, separate customer gateway device removes this single point of failure by providing an alternate physical path.

explain: Adding a second set of VPN connections from the Management VPC to a second customer gateway device provides redundancy and eliminates this single point of failure.

q: A company runs its applications on Amazon EC2 instances. The company performs periodic financial assessments of its AWS costs. The company recently identified unusual spending. The company needs a solution to prevent unusual spending. The solution must monitor costs and notify responsible stakeholders in the event of unusual spending. Which solution will meet these requirements?

o.t: Use Amazon CloudWatch to monitor costs and to identify unusual spending.
o.w: Amazon CloudWatch can monitor metrics and trigger alarms, but it has no built-in machine-learning-based cost anomaly detection; configuring it to flag "unusual" spending requires significant custom metric and threshold work.

o.t: Create an AWS Cost Anomaly Detection monitor in the AWS Billing and Cost Management console.
o.w: AWS Cost Anomaly Detection uses machine learning to automatically learn normal spending patterns and alert stakeholders when spending deviates unexpectedly, directly meeting the requirement to monitor and notify on unusual spending with minimal setup.

o.t: Use an AWS Budgets template to create a zero spend budget.
o.w: A zero-spend budget alerts only when any spending occurs at all, which is not useful for an environment that is expected to have ongoing EC2 costs; it does not detect unusual deviations from normal spending.

o.t: Create AWS Pricing Calculator estimates for the current running workload pricing details.
o.w: AWS Pricing Calculator is used to estimate the cost of a planned workload before deployment; it does not monitor actual ongoing spending or detect anomalies in real usage.

q: An ecommerce company uses Amazon Route 53 as its DNS provider. The company hosts its website on premises and in the AWS Cloud. The company's on-premises data center is near the us-west-1 Region. The company uses the eu-central-1 Region to host the website. The company wants to minimize load time for the website as much as possible. Which solution will meet these requirements?

o.t: Set up a simple routing policy that routes all traffic that is near eu-central-1 to eu-central-1 and routes all traffic that is near the on-premises datacenter to the on-premises data center.
o.w: A simple routing policy does not use geographic proximity to route users, so it cannot direct traffic based on the users' location relative to us-west-1 versus eu-central-1 the way this requirement calls for.

o.t: Set up a geolocation routing policy. Send the traffic that is near us-west-1 to the on-premises data center. Send the traffic that is near eucentral-1 to eu-central-1.
o.w: A geolocation routing policy routes traffic based on the geographic location of the requester, sending nearby on-premises-area traffic to the on-premises data center (near us-west-1) and traffic near eu-central-1 to that Region, minimizing load time for each group of users based on physical proximity.

o.t: Set up a weighted routing policy. Split the traffic evenly between eu-central-1 and the on-premises data center.
o.w: A weighted routing policy splits traffic by a fixed percentage regardless of where the user actually is, so it does not route each user to their nearest endpoint and would not minimize load time as required.

o.t: Set up a latency routing policy. Associate the policy with us-west-1.
o.w: A latency-based routing policy routes based on measured network latency between resources in different Regions, but it cannot route to the on-premises data center as an endpoint type the way a geolocation-based policy explicitly can for this on-premises/eu-central-1 split.

explain: Geolocation routing directs traffic based on the geographic location of the user. This option would send users near us-west-1 to the on-premises data center and users near eu-central-1 to eu-central-1. While this approach considers geographic location, it might not always result in the lowest latency.

q: A company seeks a storage solution for its application. The solution must be highly available and scalable. The solution also must function as a file system be mountable by multiple Linux instances in AWS and on premises through native protocols, and have no minimum size requirements. The company has set up a Site-to-Site VPN for access from its on-premises network to its VPC. Which storage solution meets these requirements?

o.t: Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) Multi-Attach volumes
o.w: EBS Multi-Attach only allows attachment to multiple EC2 instances within the same Availability Zone in a single Region, and EBS volumes are block storage with a provisioned minimum size — not natively mountable from on-premises servers and not usable as a true multi-host file system across sites.

o.t: Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) with multiple mount targets
o.w: Amazon EFS with multiple mount targets provides a shared, elastic file system that can be mounted concurrently by many Linux instances in AWS and on-premises (via the Site-to-Site VPN) using native NFS, scales automatically with no minimum size requirement, and is highly available across multiple AZs.

o.t: Amazon FSx Multi-AZ deployments
o.w: FSx Multi-AZ deployments are built around Windows File Server (SMB) or other specific file system protocols rather than a generic natively-mountable Linux file system across mixed AWS and on-premises environments, and do not match the described "native protocol, Linux-mountable, no minimum size" requirements as well as EFS.

o.t: Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) with a single mount target and multiple access points
o.w: A single mount target limits the file system to one Availability Zone, undermining the high-availability requirement; access points control permission/path scoping for NFS clients but do not provide the AZ redundancy that multiple mount targets do.

explain:
Amazon EFS is a scalable file storage service that can be mounted by multiple Amazon EC2 instances and on-premises servers.
It provides a shared file system with multiple mount targets in different Availability Zones (AZs) for high availability.
Multiple mount targets allow you to mount the file system from different subnets, ensuring that instances in different network segments can access the file system.

q: A company will migrate 10 PB of data to Amazon S3 in 6 weeks. The current data center has a 500 Mbps uplink to the internet. Other on-premises applications share the uplink. The company can use 80% of the internet bandwidth for this one-time migration task. Which solution will meet these requirements?

o.t: Configure AWS DataSync to migrate the data to Amazon S3 and to automatically verify the data.
o.w: AWS DataSync is designed for online data transfer over a network connection; given the shared, limited 500 Mbps uplink and the 6-week deadline for 10 PB, online transfer—even with verification—would take far too long and consume too much of the shared bandwidth.

o.t: Use the AWS CLI and multiple copy processes to send the data directly to Amazon S3.
o.w: Using the AWS CLI to copy 10 PB over a 500 Mbps uplink (further limited to 80% availability and shared with other applications) would take many months, far exceeding the 6-week deadline, regardless of how many parallel copy processes are used.

o.t: Use rsync to transfer the data directly to Amazon S3.
o.w: Using rsync over the same constrained 500 Mbps shared internet uplink has the same fundamental bandwidth limitation as the CLI approach, making it impractical to move 10 PB within 6 weeks.

o.t: Order multiple AWS Snowball devices. Copy the data to the devices. Send the devices to AWS to copy the data to Amazon S3.
o.w: AWS Snowball provides physical devices that bypass the limited network uplink entirely; ordering enough devices in parallel to hold 10 PB and shipping them to AWS is the only practical way to meet the 6-week deadline given the available bandwidth.

explain: With only a 500 Mbps uplink bandwidth shared among other on-premises applications, transferring 10 PB of data over the internet would be impractical and time-consuming. AWS Snowball provides a physical device that can be shipped to the company to facilitate faster initial data transfer.
